section_summary: Brazilian press clippings describe attacks on Japanese residents who accepted Japan’s defeat and unrest in Japanese communities in São Paulo state. U.S. consular, State Department, and FBI records examine Shindo Renmei, competing explanations for the violence, and efforts to distribute reliable news from Japan. The section also includes correspondence about restoring personal communication with Japan and proposals to send an official emissary.

subfiles.title: Attack on Chuzaburo Nomura and Shigetsuna Furuya
subfiles.about: Reports the murder of Chuzaburo Nomura, an attempt on former diplomat Shigetsuna Furuya, and suspected anti-defeat fanaticism.
subfiles.summary: Interviews and crime reporting describe armed intruders, family witnesses, recovered clothing, and police investigations. The clipping links the attacks to Japanese residents who rejected news of Japan’s defeat; page 57 repeats much of page 56.

subfiles.title: Em Tupã a situação não é melhor que a de Bastos
subfiles.about: Describes unrest, policing, military presence, and Japanese commemorations in Tupã and nearby towns.
subfiles.summary: The article alleges intimidation by Japanese nationalists, recounts a confrontation at the Tupã police station, and calls for stronger police and army facilities. It also reports a closed Japanese school and wartime commemorations.

subfiles.title: Um crime covarde na cidade de Bastos
subfiles.about: Discusses the murder of cooperative superintendent Ikuta Mizobe amid conflict over Japan’s surrender.
subfiles.summary: The article gives Bastos’s settlement history, describes false surrender photographs and local Japanese organizations, and links threats against Mizobe to his acceptance of defeat. It reports the murder and police inquiry while advancing allegations about nationalist societies.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-90 on informing Japanese residents of Brazil, partial copy
subfiles.about: Proposes correspondence and Japanese newspapers to counter denial of Japan’s surrender.
subfiles.summary: A partial first page outlines family correspondence and newspaper subscriptions; another copy appears on pages 76–77.

subfiles.title: Imperial rescript and Asahi copies
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, São Paulo
subfiles.about: Forwards photographic copies of Hirohito’s January 1946 rescript and an Asahi newspaper page.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Japanese-language evidence that the emperor denied his divinity.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-76: Text of the Imperial Rescript
subfiles.from: Secretary of State James F. Byrnes
subfiles.about: Supplies an English translation of Hirohito’s January 1, 1946 rescript.
subfiles.summary: The rescript recalls the Meiji Charter Oath, acknowledges Japan’s defeat and wartime suffering, calls for peaceful reconstruction, and rejects the claim that the emperor is divine or that Japanese people are destined to rule other races.

subfiles.title: Telegram 102 requesting Japanese surrender statements
subfiles.about: Requests the emperor’s proclamation and reproducible Japanese texts confirming defeat.
subfiles.summary: Brazilian authorities seek Japanese-language statements for photographic distribution.

subfiles.title: Telegram 103 appealing for information staff
subfiles.about: Warns that nationalist violence and inadequate U.S. information staffing threaten the Japanese community.
subfiles.summary: The consul reports two murders, repression of suspected extremists, and an urgent need for information personnel.

subfiles.title: FBI letter on secret Japanese societies
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports arrests after Japanese murders in Brazil and cautions that the societies’ responsibility remains unproved.
subfiles.summary: Hoover notes roughly 140 arrests, police protection for threatened residents, and possible political motives within the colony.

subfiles.title: Withdrawal notice
subfiles.about: Marks a file item withdrawn for restricted access.
subfiles.summary: A blank withdrawal form cites classified or otherwise restricted information.

subfiles.title: Reply on forwarding letters to Japan
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, São Paulo
subfiles.about: Declines a special exception for six letters to Japan pending a general mail policy decision.
subfiles.summary: Returns the letters and advises reliance on current efforts to distribute reliable news from Japan.

subfiles.title: Despatch 3933: Request that letters be forwarded to Japan
subfiles.from: Cecil M. P. Cross, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Seeks delivery of six letters from Furuya and Okinaga to contacts in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross describes Furuya’s work distributing newspapers and opposing violent secret societies, including an attempt on his life. He lists Japanese addressees and encloses six letters.

subfiles.title: Telegram 110 on arrests and land fraud
subfiles.about: Reports arrests, false claims about Japan’s victory, and fraudulent sales of Asian land and passage.
subfiles.summary: The consul says the situation remains threatening and again requests information resources.

subfiles.title: Telegram 250 requesting Tokyo newspapers
subfiles.about: Requests regular copies of five Tokyo daily newspapers for Japanese residents in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Orders newspapers sent by pouch to the São Paulo consulate, which will reimburse costs.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-90: Measures for Japanese residents in Brazil
subfiles.about: Reviews correspondence, newspapers, publicity, repatriation, and film resources for the Japanese community.
subfiles.summary: The Department seeks names for family correspondence and arranges newspaper subscriptions. It favors distributing surrender documents and the emperor’s rescript, declines a Swedish emissary, considers repatriating dangerous society leaders, and identifies available newsreels and photographs.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal on secret Japanese societies
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards an FBI report on Japanese nationalist societies in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: The letter distributes the enclosed investigation to State and military intelligence offices.

subfiles.title: Secret Japanese Societies in Brazil
subfiles.about: Investigates Shindo Renmei, associated organizations, threats, fraud allegations, and the murder of Ikuta Mizobe.
subfiles.summary: The report names society officers and local branches, describes fraudulent claims about conquered territories and yen, and presents accounts of the Bastos cooperative dispute and Mizobe’s murder. Sources disagree over whether nationalist militants, cooperative rivals, or business conflicts caused the killing. The report records threatened residents and a youth strike group but repeatedly notes that a direct link between that group, Shindo Renmei, and the murder had not been proved.

subfiles.title: Routing note for Benton reply
subfiles.about: Requests a prompt reply for Benton’s signature.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten note discusses signature arrangements during officers’ absence.

subfiles.title: Telegram 122 on Japanese tensions and wheat protests
subfiles.about: Reports continuing Japanese tensions and protests over false claims about Argentine wheat.
subfiles.summary: The consul asks about Paul van Orden Shaw’s appointment amid growing need for information work.

subfiles.title: Despatch 3950 transmitting a political report
subfiles.from: Cecil M. P. Cross, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Transmits correspondence on the Japanese situation in São Paulo.
subfiles.summary: Cover despatch forwards a letter previously sent to the Rio de Janeiro embassy.

subfiles.title: Letter on the Japanese situation in São Paulo
subfiles.from: Cecil M. P. Cross, American Consul General
subfiles.to: Paul C. Daniels, American Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Describes prisoner overcrowding and efforts to circulate the emperor’s surrender rescript.
subfiles.summary: Cross reports that police may release detainees and says Swedish circulars and Portuguese newspaper translations are being distributed. He asks for occupation films.

subfiles.title: Despatch 394: Newspapers for Japanese Residents of Brazil
subfiles.about: Reports initial shipment and planned regular delivery of Japanese newspapers to São Paulo.
subfiles.summary: Three copies of five editions were sent; two copies of five Tokyo dailies will follow regularly.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice
subfiles.from: Department of State, Communications and Records
subfiles.about: Designates a white copy as the record copy of a telegram or airgram.
subfiles.summary: The white copy replaces a yellow action copy missing from Central Records.

subfiles.title: Telegram 144 requesting the rescript and newspapers
subfiles.about: Asks when the Japanese rescript text and Tokyo newspapers will arrive.
subfiles.summary: The consul describes the local situation as still tense and deteriorating.

subfiles.title: Despatch 3977: Communication with Japan
subfiles.from: Cecil M. P. Cross, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Forwards missionary correspondence and a Japanese leaders’ memorial seeking communication with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross argues that censored personal letters could weaken belief in Japan’s victory and warns that terrorism may continue.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Japanese newspapers
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, São Paulo
subfiles.about: Encloses late-April and early-May Japanese newspapers concerning Japan’s surrender.
subfiles.summary: Lists Asahi, Yomiuri, and Mainichi editions and promises further surrender material.

subfiles.title: Telegram 152 on proposals to confirm Japan’s defeat
subfiles.about: Relays Japanese leaders’ proposals for an official emissary, fact-finding mission, and personal correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The consul reports that Brazilian authorities released most detainees and that some residents misread this as Japanese government pressure. He asks again for occupation photographs, films, and current newspapers.

subfiles.title: Byron S. Lamson’s letter on Japanese residents in Brazil
subfiles.to: Secretary of State James F. Byrnes
subfiles.about: Urges an authoritative Japanese statement in Brazil and presents Massao Kinoshita as a possible emissary.
subfiles.summary: Lamson says many Japanese residents cannot read Portuguese or English and have been deceived into buying false passage and land claims. He endorses Kinoshita, cites pastor Daniel Nishizumi’s support, and asks the State Department to help arrange a trip to Japan.
